text: A Turing machine has an infinite tape. Since no real machine does, why is the model still relevant?
choices: Real machines approximate it closely enough, since modern memory is effectively unbounded.
It is not relevant in practice; it survives for historical reasons in theory courses.
It is relevant because real processors are implemented internally as Turing machines.
It marks the boundary of what is computable at all, and no real machine can exceed it — the tape's infinity only removes a memory limit, not a capability limit.
explanation: The point of the infinite tape is to make the model about *computability* rather than about capacity. A result proved for Turing machines — such as Chapter 34's undecidability of halting — applies to every real machine, because a real machine can do strictly less. The infinity makes the negative results stronger, not weaker, which is the opposite of the usual intuition about idealised models.
